diagnosis.what_is_wrong: The trace shows a short, compute-heavy task run, but does not establish a host fault or explain an abnormal slowdown: ttworker consumed nearly four CPU-seconds per second while the task was active, then stopped, with no reported evidence of scheduler starvation, problematic disk latency, or a synchronized host-wide failure. The operator’s symptom cannot be confirmed as a fault from this trace alone; I classify it as normal rather than attributing the task’s own CPU work to an external cause.
diagnosis.evidence: Compared the reported Python-derived sched_stat_runtime totals across the aligned quiet-ish interval 02:47:30.200–02:47:31.200 and worker interval 02:47:31.200–02:47:35.200: container pid_ns 4026531836 rose from 82.39 ms CPU in the preceding second to 15,749.34 ms over the next four seconds, of which ttworker used 15,228.02 ms (96.7%). It then fell to 235.49 ms in 02:47:35.200–02:47:36.200; ttworker’s exit was recorded at 02:47:35.382. ctf_proclife associates the run_all.sh/worker cohort with this boundary. ctf_timeline did not match recorded event names, so workers reconstructed rates from the indexed dataframe; those show no broad synchronized collapse/recovery. Reported raw sched_switch samples show normal-priority tasks and prev_state=0; sampled block completions report error=0 and sampled net_dev_xmit records rc=0. These checks do not prove all wait was absent, but they provide no positive evidence for a separate bottleneck. The notes contain no ctf_procdiff result and no measured comparison to a known-good coding-task run.
diagnosis.window_evidence: This is the observed task/compute-burst window, not a confirmed fault interval: the aligned CPU totals jump at 02:47:31.200 when the worker cohort becomes active, remain near four CPU-seconds per second through 02:47:35.200, then fall sharply; the raw sched_process_exit for ttworker TID 3480 is at 02:47:35.382. The preceding 02:47:30.200–02:47:31.200 interval is the comparison window, not an established historical baseline.
